analysis.one_liner: Creates a guaranteed basic health insurance package for everyone, with market rules, rural clinician incentives, and malpractice limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote: introduced in May 1992 with one cosponsor, it was referred to four House committees and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require insurers to sell a standard 'BasiCare' plan to anyone who applies, regardless of health, with community-wide rates and a ban on charging sick people more. It would expand community health center grants, fully make health insurance premiums deductible for the self-employed, and offer tax breaks to clinicians who serve rural shortage areas. It would also cap malpractice awards at $250,000 for pain and suffering, limit hospital antitrust liability for joint ventures, and finance universal coverage through a fund built from a share of wages, with Medicaid coverage phased out after five years in favor of subsidized private plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured people would gain guaranteed access to a standard benefits package with caps on deductibles and out-of-pocket costs, no exclusions for preexisting conditions after six months, and full preventive coverage for children and pregnant women [S2] [S3]. Small employers and the self-employed would get guaranteed-issue insurance and a 100% deduction for premiums [S2]. Low-income people would receive vouchers for premiums and cost-sharing [S2]. Rural communities would gain expanded National Health Service Corps funding and tax credits for clinicians who practice in shortage areas [S2] [S3]. Federally qualified health centers would receive $600 million per year in grants for fiscal years 1993-1997 [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: The uninsured, small employers, rural patients

how_it_helps.text: Every insurer would have to offer a BasiCare plan to any applicant, with guaranteed renewability, limits on preexisting-condition exclusions to six months, and community-wide ratings prohibiting health-based pricing [S2] [S3].

Small-employer plans could not carry deductibles above $500 per individual or out-of-pocket costs above $2,000, and children under 23 and pregnant women would receive specified preventive services with no deductibles or coinsurance [S3].

The bill would authorize $600 million annually for fiscal years 1993 through 1997 to expand federally qualified health centers and community-based primary care for low-income and medically underserved populations [S3].
Self-employed individuals could deduct 100% of health insurance costs, up from 25%, permanently [S2] [S3].

Clinicians serving rural health professional shortage areas would get a tax credit of up to $1,000 per month for up to 36 months, tax-free National Health Service Corps loan repayments, larger equipment expensing, and student-loan interest deductions [S3].
Low-income individuals would receive financial assistance through a voucher system for BasiCare premiums, deductibles, and other cost-sharing [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Wage earners and the self-employed would finance the system through a specified percentage of wages and self-employment income transferred to the BasiCare Trust Fund, which would also absorb unobligated Medicare trust fund balances and take over the federal Medicaid share [S2]. Insurers offering non-qualifying plans would face an excise tax of 35% of gross premiums, employers and providers would face compliance taxes, and individuals who failed to report a BasiCare policy number would lose their personal tax exemption [S2] [S3]. Patients injured by negligent care would lose some legal remedies: noneconomic damages capped at $250,000, awards offset by other compensation received, and strict time limits on filing [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers through payroll contributions; injured patients

drawbacks.text: The malpractice title would cap total noneconomic damages at $250,000 per injured person and their family regardless of how many providers were at fault, require offset of damages by any other compensation received, cap single payments at $100,000, and preempt state laws that allow greater recovery [S3] — patients with the most severe injuries from negligence would bear the cost.
Financing would come from a percentage of wages and self-employment income flowing into the BasiCare Trust Fund, a broad levy on work rather than on wealth or profits [S2].

Medicaid would be terminated after five years for benefits duplicating or subsumed by BasiCare, with low-income people shifted to vouchers for private coverage — a risk if BasiCare premiums or benefits proved inadequate [S2].
The bill would preempt inconsistent state insurance and tort laws, overriding stronger consumer protections some states had already enacted [S2] [S3].

Much of the actual program design — the benefits package, premium levels, and the legislative proposal for universal coverage — would be delegated to a new Commission to propose in future years, with Congress considering it under expedited procedures, so passage alone would not have delivered the final system [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The coverage guarantees, health center expansion, and rural clinician incentives would have delivered real gains to uninsured and underserved people, and the small-market insurance rules anticipated consumer protections that later became law. But the bill asked workers to finance universal coverage through a broad payroll-based levy, sharply limited the legal rights of patients harmed by negligent care, exempted hospital joint ventures from antitrust scrutiny, and left the hardest design choices to a future commission. The malpractice title in particular traded patient recovery for provider relief without a parallel guarantee that savings would be passed to patients.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 1992, sent to four House committees, and referred to subcommittees, but no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Dan Glickman introduced the BasiCare Health Access and Cost Control Act on May 14, 1992, joined by Rep. Dave McCurdy as its only cosponsor [S3] [S4].
The same day, it was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Rules — a multi-committee referral that gave any single panel the power to hold it [S5].

In May and June 1992 it was referred to subcommittees on Economic and Commercial Law, Health and the Environment, and Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill received no floor vote in either chamber and died on January 3, 1993, when the 102nd Congress ended [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and medical providers were better off: they avoided guaranteed-issue requirements, community rating, a 35% excise tax on non-qualifying plans, malpractice litigation limits that had been packaged with them, and hospital antitrust restrictions. Americans without adequate health insurance gained nothing from the bill's death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and providers; the uninsured gained nothing

sides.party_line_note: Both sponsors were Democrats and no Republican cosponsored, but no vote was ever taken, so the bill's partisan support on the floor was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would force every carrier to sell a standardized, community-rated BasiCare plan and tax non-qualifying plans at 35% of premiums, ending health-based underwriting — but it would also make private insurers the permanent, mandatory channel for everyone's coverage, financed through a public trust fund, with every individual required to hold a policy. Insurers would lose rating freedom but gain a guaranteed, subsidized customer base.

Providers would gain a $250,000 cap on noneconomic malpractice damages, collateral-source offsets, an antitrust exemption for hospital joint ventures, and tens of millions of newly insured paying customers. They would pay compliance taxes and participate in BasiCare on regulated terms. The malpractice and antitrust provisions run against patients; the new covered population runs with them.
Capped damages, court-controlled attorney fees, and shortened filing deadlines would sharply reduce malpractice contingency work — the same provisions that would reduce recovery for injured patients.
The bill would authorize $600 million per year for fiscal years 1993-1997 to expand community health centers serving low-income and medically underserved populations.
Universal coverage including prescription drugs would expand the paying market, while the Commission would be required to submit a legislative proposal for affordable access to prescription drugs.
